claims.text: Dynamic deformation-induced amorphization can produce an ultra-nanocrystalline amorphous layer at grain boundaries in high-entropy alloys.
This grain-boundary layer governs hardness and strength.
Formation of this layer leads to inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
CoCrFeMnNi can be prepared as a single-phase, coarse-grained high-entropy alloy.
Severe plastic deformation will induce nanograins and trigger dynamic amorphization.
Annealing can maintain a mostly coarse-grained baseline that suppresses dynamic amorphization.
An inert environment avoids oxidation-related changes to deformation and tribological behavior.
A thin ultra-nanocrystalline amorphous grain-boundary layer alters local shear strength.
Under applied stress, grain boundaries in coarse-grained regions undergo localized amorphization.
The resulting layer raises shear resistance.
The resulting layer hardens the material.
The resulting layer reduces friction.
Samples displaying dynamic amorphization will have greater hardness than the coarse-grained baseline.
Samples displaying dynamic amorphization will have lower friction coefficients than the coarse-grained baseline.
The deformed samples will deviate from classical Hall-Petch behavior.
The proposed behavior is limited to single-phase high-entropy alloys under inert conditions.
The proposed behavior may not hold in multiphase materials.
The proposed behavior may not hold in oxidizing environments because surface chemistry alters deformation behavior.
The magnitude of hardness enhancement depends on grain-size distribution and alloy composition.
Failure to detect the layer, or retention of classical Hall-Petch behavior without increased hardness or reduced friction, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed layer is called both ultra-nanocrystalline and amorphous. These are structurally distinct descriptions unless the layer is explicitly defined as a mixed nanocrystalline-amorphous structure.

The baseline is described as coarse-grained to suppress dynamic amorphization, while the mechanism states that grain boundaries in coarse-grained regions undergo localized amorphization under applied stress; the conditions distinguishing suppression from activation are not specified.
